verses.text: Yahweh said to Moses in Mount Sinai,
“Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘When you come into the land which I give you, then the land shall keep a Sabbath to Yahweh.
You shall sow your field six years, and you shall prune your vineyard six years, and gather in its fruits;
but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to Yahweh. You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard.
What grows of itself in your harvest you shall not reap, and you shall not gather the grapes of your undressed vine. It shall be a year of solemn rest for the land.
The Sabbath of the land shall be for food for you; for yourself, for your servant, for your maid, for your hired servant, and for your stranger, who lives as a foreigner with you.
For your livestock also, and for the animals that are in your land, shall all its increase be for food.
“‘You shall count off seven Sabbaths of years, seven times seven years; and there shall be to you the days of seven Sabbaths of years, even forty-nine years.
Then you shall sound the loud trumpet on the tenth day of the seventh month. On the Day of Atonement you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land.

You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.
That fiftieth year shall be a jubilee to you. In it you shall not sow, neither reap that which grows of itself, nor gather from the undressed vines.
For it is a jubilee; it shall be holy to you. You shall eat of its increase out of the field.
“‘In this Year of Jubilee each of you shall return to his property.
“‘If you sell anything to your neighbor, or buy from your neighbor, you shall not wrong one another.
According to the number of years after the Jubilee you shall buy from your neighbor. According to the number of years of the crops he shall sell to you.
According to the length of the years you shall increase its price, and according to the shortness of the years you shall diminish its price; for he is selling the number of the crops to you.
You shall not wrong one another; but you shall fear your God: for I am Yahweh your God.
“‘Therefore you shall do my statutes, and keep my ordinances and do them; and you shall dwell in the land in safety.
The land shall yield its fruit, and you shall eat your fill, and dwell therein in safety.
If you said, “What shall we eat the seventh year? Behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase”;
then I will command my blessing on you in the sixth year, and it shall bear fruit for the three years.
You shall sow the eighth year, and eat of the fruits, the old store; until the ninth year, until its fruits come in, you shall eat the old store.
“‘The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine; for you are strangers and live as foreigners with me.
In all the land of your possession you shall grant a redemption for the land.
“‘If your brother becomes poor, and sells some of his possessions, then his kinsman who is next to him shall come, and redeem that which his brother has sold.
If a man has no one to redeem it, and he becomes prosperous and finds sufficient means to redeem it;
then let him reckon the years since its sale, and restore the surplus to the man to whom he sold it; and he shall return to his property.

But if he isn’t able to get it back for himself, then what he has sold shall remain in the hand of him who has bought it until the Year of Jubilee: and in the Jubilee it shall be released, and he shall return to his property.
“‘If a man sells a dwelling house in a walled city, then he may redeem it within a whole year after it has been sold. For a full year he shall have the right of redemption.

If it isn’t redeemed within the space of a full year, then the house that is in the walled city shall be made sure in perpetuity to him who bought it, throughout his generations. It shall not be released in the Jubilee.
But the houses of the villages which have no wall around them shall be accounted for with the fields of the country: they may be redeemed, and they shall be released in the Jubilee.
“‘Nevertheless the cities of the Levites, the houses in the cities of their possession, the Levites may redeem at any time.

The Levites may redeem the house that was sold, and the city of his possession, and it shall be released in the Jubilee; for the houses of the cities of the Levites are their possession among the children of Israel.
But the field of the suburbs of their cities may not be sold; for it is their perpetual possession.
“‘If your brother has become poor, and his hand can’t support himself among you; then you shall uphold him. He shall live with you like an alien and a temporary resident.
Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God; that your brother may live among you.
You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit.
I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan, and to be your God.
“‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave.
As a hired servant, and as a temporary resident, he shall be with you; he shall serve with you until the Year of Jubilee:
then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and shall return to his own family, and to the possession of his fathers.
For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be sold as slaves.
You shall not rule over him with harshness, but shall fear your God.
“‘As for your male and your female slaves, whom you may have; of the nations that are around you, from them you may buy male and female slaves.
Moreover of the children of the aliens who live among you, of them you may buy, and of their families who are with you, which they have conceived in your land; and they will be your property.

You may make them an inheritance for your children after you, to hold for a possession; of them may you take your slaves forever; but over your brothers the children of Israel you shall not rule, one over another, with harshness.

“‘If an alien or temporary resident with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him has grown poor, and sells himself to the stranger or foreigner living among you, or to a member of the stranger’s family;
after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him;
or his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any who is a close relative to him of his family may redeem him; or if he has grown rich, he may redeem himself.

He shall reckon with him who bought him from the year that he sold himself to him to the Year of Jubilee. The price of his sale shall be according to the number of years; he shall be with him according to the time of a hired servant.
If there are yet many years, according to them he shall give back the price of his redemption out of the money that he was bought for.
If there remain but a few years to the year of jubilee, then he shall reckon with him; according to his years of service he shall give back the price of his redemption.
As a servant hired year by year shall he be with him. He shall not rule with harshness over him in your sight.
If he isn’t redeemed by these means, then he shall be released in the Year of Jubilee, he, and his children with him.
For to me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks from Mount Sinai—a place where Moses already received the Ten Commandments. Now He gives laws that shape how His people will rest and remember. Every word here is meant to order a whole society around trust in His provision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The land itself will keep Sabbath to the Lord—not the people only. Land is never mere property; it belongs to God and needs rest just as we do. This inverts how most kingdoms think: the land is holy ground, not a resource to exhaust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six years of sowing and pruning: hard, faithful work. The Lord doesn't call us to idleness but to honest labor. Yet even in our striving, we're kept inside a rhythm—one that ensures we won't burn ourselves hollow in the pursuit of plenty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The seventh year, land lies fallow. No sowing, no pruning—only waiting. This takes enormous faith from a farmer. But God teaches: I own this ground, not you. Your security comes from trusting Me, not from straining to wring out every harvest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What grows by itself is not yours to harvest. Leave it for the poor, the stranger, your animals—those with no other recourse. Sabbath rest turns into Sabbath mercy. The untended field becomes a school in generosity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Sabbath yield feeds everyone—you, servants, hired workers, strangers. No one is shut out. This law is breathtaking: the land's rest becomes a feast that gathers the whole community, high and low, native and alien, all sustained together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even livestock eat from the Sabbath abundance. Creation itself is held in the Sabbath rhythm—a gentle word that animals matter too, that God's rest is not just for humans. Mercy extends far and wide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Count seven sevens—forty-nine years of Sabbaths. Each one a small act of faith; together they build toward something far larger. God thinks in long rhythms. He is patient, and He teaches us patience by asking us to count and wait.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The trumpet on the Day of Atonement announces the Jubilee to all the land. Forgiveness and freedom are linked: guilt is cleared, and the land returns home. The sound travels everywhere—no one is forgotten.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Liberty is proclaimed to all inhabitants—the poor, the enslaved, all who have lost their place. The Jubilee is not a suggestion; it is a decree written into the calendar itself. God does not allow debt to harden into dynasty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jubilee year is holy—set apart, unremarkable in its fields and vines yet full of meaning. You do not sow or reap; you simply live as a guest on God's land, holding nothing back, waiting on His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eat from the field's yield in the Jubilee—what it gives of itself. This is the paradox of trust: you work hard for six cycles, then you rest and receive. The land feeds you when you stop trying to force it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each returns to his property. Not by purchase or struggle, but by the Lord's calendar. No one is meant to be uprooted forever. God's justice includes the right to come home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Do not wrong one another in selling or buying. Fair dealing is not optional; it is commanded. Every transaction is a place where the fear of God shows itself in honest weights and kind words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Price a sale by the years until Jubilee—not by the land's potential alone, but by time. The closer the Jubilee, the lower the price. This is ingenious: it prevents wealth from concentrating and ensures the poor always have a path to restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Price reflects the years of crops you are selling—a fair measure. The law here is arithmetic and also grace: the system itself is shaped to keep generosity alive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Do not wrong one another; fear your God. Here the fear of the Lord is the cure for greed. When you remember that He sees every deal and judges every heart, dishonesty becomes unthinkable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Keep the statutes and ordinances, and you shall dwell in safety. Obedience here is not about earning favor; it is about aligning yourself with how God has ordered the world. Injustice breeds insecurity; righteousness brings peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The land yields its fruit, you eat your fill, and dwell in safety. This is the promise—not wealth beyond measure, but enough, and the deep rest of knowing you are secure. More than abundance: contentment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You ask, What shall we eat? Fear whispers into your ear in the Sabbath year. The question is honest, born from real vulnerability. But God does not dismiss it; He meets it with a promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will command my blessing in the sixth year. The Lord does not leave you to guess. In the year before Sabbath rest, He provides double blessing—a tangible word that He will care for you. This is how faith grows: by experience of His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You sow in the eighth year and eat old stores until the new crop comes. The Lord's provision bridges the gap. This is no magic but faithful stewardship meeting divine promise. You are never abandoned in the lean season.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for it is mine. You are strangers and live as foreigners with me. The Lord owns the earth; you are tenant. This frees you from the illusion that land can be your fortress—only God can be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You shall grant a redemption for the land—a legal right to restore what was lost. The law itself is an instrument of mercy. God writes paths back home into the very structure of how His people deal with each other.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If your brother becomes poor and sells, his kinsman shall redeem. The family does not abandon its own to permanent loss. Redemption is not charity but duty—love made legal and binding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If a man has no one to redeem it but later becomes prosperous, he may restore what he lost. God's law leaves room for a man's own redemption. Poverty is not the final word; the path to recovery is written in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reckon the years, restore the surplus, and he shall return to his property. Justice is detailed here—precise, fair, meant to restore the seller to his rightful place. The law is not abstract but applied with care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he cannot redeem it, it remains with the buyer until Jubilee, then is released. Even if the poor man cannot restore himself in his lifetime, the law ensures the next generation receives a fresh start. God thinks in generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A dwelling house in a walled city may be redeemed within a full year. Urban property has different rules than land—a whole year to restore what was sold in haste. God's law recognizes how pressure and desperation cloud our choices.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If unredeemed, the house belongs to the buyer in perpetuity. Urban housing, unlike land, does not return in Jubilee. The law treats the settled places differently—acknowledging that a city house is a different kind of holding than ancestral land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Houses of villages without walls are accounted as fields and released in Jubilee. In smaller, open places, the land's rhythm prevails. God's law keeps communities rooted and flexible according to their nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Levites—God's servants—may redeem their city houses at any time. They have a special right because they serve at the Lord's altar. Even the law of property bows to the holiness that belongs to His worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Levite houses and cities are released in Jubilee—their possessions are given back. The Levites, who have no tribal inheritance, are held secure by God Himself. He is their portion and their inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fields around Levite cities cannot be sold—they remain their perpetual possession. A boundary is drawn: the Levites' livelihood is protected so they can serve. God does not ask His ministers to starve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If your brother becomes poor and his hand cannot support him, you shall uphold him as an alien and temporary resident. He belongs to the community but is vulnerable. The law calls you to hold him up until he can stand again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take no interest, charge no profit—fear your God so that your brother may live. Lending to the poor is an act of worship. The fear of God shows itself in how you treat the desperate: with open hands, not grasping ones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Do not lend money at interest or give food for profit to those in need. Every verse underlines the same truth: compassion is not negotiable, not something to squeeze value from. The poor have a claim on the rich born from God's character.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of Egypt and gave you Canaan. The Lord grounds His call to mercy in His own rescue of you. You were once enslaved; He set you free. Now extend that same mercy to others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If your brother becomes poor and sells himself, you shall not make him to serve as a slave. Even poverty's desperation does not buy the right to enslave an Israelite. Some things God forbids entirely—the human person is not merchandise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shall be with you as a hired servant, as a temporary resident, until Jubilee. Work replaces slavery; temporary replaces permanent. This law restores dignity: he earns his keep, is not property, and has a day of release written before him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shall go out with his children and return to his own family and fathers' possession in Jubilee. The bond is broken, the family is reunited, the ancestral inheritance is restored. No debt lasts beyond the generation that incurred it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They are my servants whom I brought out of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves. All Israelites belong to God alone. They are already redeemed; their status as the Lord's own people cannot be cancelled by any contract.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Do not rule over him with harshness; fear your God. Even legal work has limits. Authority must be tempered with mercy. The fear of God is the leash that keeps power from becoming cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You may buy male and female slaves from the nations around you. The law permits slavery of foreigners—a boundary the Lord draws. Israelites, being God's own people, have a different status than those outside the covenant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the alien children who live among you, you may buy and hold as property for your heirs. Foreign slaves and their children born in the land may be inherited. A hard word, yet within an ancient framework of what vassalage and contract meant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These you may hold forever; but brothers you shall not rule with harshness. The line is absolute: Israelites and foreigners are treated under different laws. Your own people retain dignity and rights; the distinction marks God's covenant and its boundaries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If an alien becomes rich and your Israelite brother becomes poor and sells himself to the foreigner, the law still steps in. Even crossing this boundary, even serving a non-Israelite, the poor man is not forgotten. God keeps track.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After he is sold, he may be redeemed—his brother may buy him back. The family's redemption right follows him even into this low place. Blood is thicker than the contracts of despair.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Uncle, uncle's son, or any close relative may redeem him—even the man himself if he becomes prosperous. The net of kinship is wide. The law multiplies the chances that someone will fight to bring him home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reckon the price by years to Jubilee—he is hired, not owned, even if sold. The pricing logic of redemption applies here too. Every arrangement, even this one, is measured and softened by the promise of Jubilee.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If many years remain until Jubilee, he must pay much to redeem himself. Time is the measure of value. The longer the years of service left, the more the redemption costs. The law is ruthless about the calculus, yet merciful about the limit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If few years remain, the price is lower. Redemption becomes possible if Jubilee is near. The law itself conspires toward freedom; the calendar works in the captive's favor as the day of release approaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He serves as a hired servant year by year; you shall not rule with harshness over him. Even at the bottom, even in servitude, a man must be treated with dignity. The law's power is that it reaches down into the hardest places and sets a floor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If unredeemed, he is released in Jubilee, he and his children with him. The Jubilee is an absolute: it stops debt in its tracks and frees the whole household. No amount of time or pressure can override God's appointed day of release.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For to me the Israelites are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of Egypt. Looking back from a longer road, readers today hear an echo: we too are brought out of slavery—not Egypt's, but sin's—and belong to God alone. As of 2026-10, I see how often the Lord's redemptive word frames every law: you are not ultimately anyone's property but His, and He keeps His promises across all generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
